openingProblem.problem: In 1947 western Europe was close to economic collapse. By 1963 West Germany was an export giant and France had a stable new republic. Was recovery made in Washington, in Bonn and Paris, or simply by the boom of the times?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what mattered most for recovery?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Europe in 1947 and the Marshall Plan
chunks.body:
Two years after the war, western Europe was close to choking. The United States had already lent large sums: $4.4 billion to Britain and $1.9 billion to France. But Tony Judt explains that these loans plugged holes rather than rebuilt economies, and they came with conditions Europe could not meet. When Truman cancelled wartime Lend-Lease, the economist John Maynard Keynes warned the British Cabinet of an "economic Dunkirk". By the spring of 1947 the bilateral approach had failed. Europe's trade deficit with the United States would reach $4,742 million in 1947, more than double the year before. Europe could not pay for the food, fuel and raw materials it needed.

On 5 June 1947, at Harvard University, Secretary of State George Marshall announced a **European Recovery Program**. The British Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, called it "one of the greatest speeches in world history". It broke with past practice. Europeans themselves would decide whether to accept American aid and how to use it. The aid would be spread over several years, a strategic programme of recovery rather than a disaster fund. And it was huge: by 1952 the United States had spent about $13 billion, more than all its previous overseas aid combined, about half of one per cent of its GDP each year from 1948 to 1951.

The offer was made to all European countries. Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov came to Paris to discuss it, but on 2 July 1947 he walked out: the conditions were incompatible with the closed Soviet economy. From 12 July sixteen western European states took part; despite early interest from Poland, Czechoslovakia and others, no future Communist state received a dollar. Within a year, Congress was persuaded that Marshall aid was "an economic barrier to Soviet expansion".

This mattered because Europe's division now had an economic form, which meant that the Marshall Plan became both a programme of recovery and a dividing line of the Cold War. In Germany, as the German question section shows, it also helped turn the western zones into a separate economy.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Marshall Plan answered a dollar crisis that threatened Europe's recovery.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some historians see a 'temporary' shortfall that would have eased anyway; Judt replies that no one could know that in 1947.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Its design, European control and multi-year funding, made it different from earlier aid.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: American advisers still played a prominent role in administering it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Soviet refusal turned the Plan into a dividing line of the Cold War.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The offer was genuinely open in June 1947; division followed from Soviet choice.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was the Marshall Plan responsible for the economic recovery of western Europe between 1947 and 1952?
Compare and contrast the recovery of West Germany and France between 1945 and 1963.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Marshall Plan was a response to a dollar crisis that threatened to stop western Europe's recovery.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Europe's trade deficit with the United States reached $4,742 million in 1947, and earlier American loans, such as $4.4 billion to Britain, had been spent within months.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that governments could not import the food and raw materials they needed without cutting living standards, so recovery itself was at risk.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, some argue that the shortfall was temporary and that European economies were already growing.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Plan was therefore crucial less because Europe could not grow without it than because no government could be sure of that in 1947.

chunks.title: What did the Marshall Plan achieve?
chunks.body:
Western Europe recovered precisely during the Marshall years. French industrial and agricultural output passed 1938 levels for the first time in 1949; West Germany and Greece reached that point in 1950. Between 1947 and 1951 the combined GNP of western Europe rose by 30 per cent. In the short term, Judt argues, the Plan's main contribution was dollars: they paid for imports such as wheat, four-fifths of which came from the dollar zone in 1949–51.

Could Europe have recovered without it? Judt accepts that it probably could have grown, but only by squeezing domestic demand, cutting the new social services and lowering living standards. That was a risk elected governments could not afford. His verdict: "The Marshall Plan was an economic program but the crisis it averted was political." By buying time, it protected fragile democracies.

Each country used the money in its own way. In **France**, Marshall dollars financed almost half of public investment under the **Monnet Plan** for modernisation. One of Jean Monnet's colleagues admitted, "we used the Americans to impose on the French government what we deemed necessary." Yet the Plan was unpopular there: in 1950 only one French adult in three had even heard of it, and 64 per cent of those thought it bad for France. In Austria, by contrast, Marshall aid provided 14 per cent of national income in its first full year.

Judt believes the deepest benefits were psychological. The Plan obliged suspicious European governments to sit down together and coordinate their policies, and it made the beggar-your-neighbour trade and currency practices of the 1930s look "first imprudent, then unnecessary and finally absurd". Cooperation soon took a European form. France's own recovery depended on German coal, and on 9 May 1950 the French Foreign Minister, Robert Schuman, proposed pooling French and German coal and steel. Konrad Adenauer welcomed it as "our breakthrough": for the first time West Germany would join an international body as an equal. In April 1951 six states founded the **European Coal and Steel Community**; Britain stayed out.

This mattered because recovery and reconciliation came together, which meant that western Europe's economic revival also bound West Germany to its neighbours.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Marshall dollars were decisive in the short term because they paid for essential imports.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Recovery had begun before the aid arrived in several countries.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Plan's greatest effect was political: it bought time for fragile democracies.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its impact on European integration was only indirect, as Judt admits.

argumentsThatWork.claim: France used the aid for its own planned modernisation, not American-style liberalisation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Plan was unpopular in France, so its political gains there were limited.

chunks.title: Adenauer and the Wirtschaftswunder
chunks.body:
West Germany's recovery became the most famous of all, the *Wirtschaftswunder* or economic miracle. In the 1950s output per head grew by an average of 6.5 per cent a year, against 0.4 per cent a year between 1913 and 1950. Between 1950 and 1973 German GDP per head more than tripled. West Germany's share of the world's exports of manufactured goods rose from 7.3 per cent in 1950 to 19.3 per cent in 1960.

Why? Part of the answer lay in what survived the war. At Volkswagen 91 per cent of the machinery had survived bombing and looting, and by 1948 the factory could make one in every two cars produced in western Germany. Part lay in the currency reform of 1948 and the Marshall years, and in the growth of world trade. And part lay in labour: of some 13 million Germans expelled from eastern Europe, nearly 9 million settled in the western zones, and more arrived through Berlin.

Judt stresses the political framework. The institutions of the Federal Republic were designed to avoid a second Weimar. Power was shared with the regional *Länder*, and the Bundestag could only remove a Chancellor if it already had a successor with a majority, which gave strong Chancellors long tenure. The "social market" economy aimed to prevent class conflict. Under the Co-Determination Law of 1951, workers sat on the supervisory boards of large coal, iron and steel firms. The state was far from absent: it controlled 40 per cent of coal and iron production and most banks. Judt notes that this regulated, cooperative economy was not what Ludwig Erhard, Adenauer's economics minister and champion of the free market, would have chosen. But a fast-growing economy let unions and employers settle disputes without conflict.

**Konrad Adenauer** presided over it all. His Christian Democrats governed without interruption from 1949 until 1966; he himself led until he resigned in 1963 at the age of 87. He built a Christian rather than a narrowly Catholic party, allied with Bavaria's CSU. Judt credits him with steering the Federal Republic between neo-Nazism and pro-Soviet neutralism and anchoring it firmly in the West. His last years were less certain: a Franco-German friendship treaty signed with de Gaulle in January 1963 alarmed his own party, which feared for the American alliance, and his colleagues removed him later that year.

This mattered because prosperity gave the new democracy legitimacy, which meant that West Germans, unlike the citizens of Weimar, associated democracy with success.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The economic miracle rested on surviving industrial capacity, labour from the expellees and booming world trade.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Policy also mattered: the currency reform and the social market.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Bonn's institutions and the social market reduced conflict and gave strong, stable government.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The economy was more regulated and cartel-like than free-market rhetoric suggested.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Adenauer anchored West Germany in the West and gave it stable leadership.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His own party removed him in 1963, partly over his closeness to de Gaulle.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the reasons for the West German economic miracle between 1948 and 1963.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The West German economic miracle rested above all on the rapid growth of exports in an expanding world economy.
useItInAnEssay.prove: West Germany's share of world exports of manufactured goods rose from 7.3 per cent in 1950 to 19.3 per cent in 1960, helped by industrial capacity such as Volkswagen's, 91 per cent of which survived the war.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that surviving factories and millions of expellee workers could be put to work selling into booming markets, so growth reached 6.5 per cent a year per head.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the social market and Co-Determination kept industrial peace, which Judt argues mattered as much as markets.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Exports were therefore the engine of the miracle, while the political framework kept it running smoothly.

chunks.title: De Gaulle: from the Fourth to the Fifth Republic
chunks.body:
France recovered economically while its politics failed. The **Fourth Republic** lasted just twelve years. Judt lists its weaknesses: no effective executive, because memories of Vichy made legislators wary of a strong president; an electoral system that produced many parties and unstable coalitions; a social backlash, seen in Pierre Poujade's protest movement, which won 52 seats in 1956; and above all, the cost of colonial wars, fought almost continuously from 1947 and, after 1955, in Algeria. Between December 1955 and December 1957 France lost two-thirds of its currency reserves, even though the economy was growing.

Algeria brought it down. In April 1958 the government fell again, the third in eleven months, and European settlers in Algiers, fearing Paris would abandon them, formed a "Committee of Public Safety" demanding de Gaulle's return. On 15 May General Salan, the army commander in Algeria, called out de Gaulle's name to a cheering crowd. Rebels seized Corsica and Paris feared a paratroop landing. On 28 May the prime minister resigned, and on 1 June Charles de Gaulle took office; the Assembly gave him full powers the next day. In Algiers he told the crowd, in a deliberately ambiguous phrase: "I have understood you".

De Gaulle's **Fifth Republic** was designed to avoid the old faults. The Assembly and the parties lost power; the President gained control of policy and the right to appoint and dismiss prime ministers. The new constitution won 80 per cent of the vote in France in September 1958. A new franc in December 1958 launched a radical economic reform. In 1962 a referendum approved the direct election of the President, giving him, Judt writes, more power than any other freely elected head of state in the world.

De Gaulle then did what the settlers had not expected. In September 1959 he proposed self-determination for Algeria. Settlers and officers rebelled: barricades in Algiers in January 1960, a failed generals' putsch in April 1961, and the terrorism of the OAS, whose bombs killed 553 people in February 1962 alone. De Gaulle negotiated with the Algerian nationalists at Evian; a ceasefire came on 19 March 1962, and after a referendum on 1 July, Algeria became independent two days later.

This mattered because de Gaulle used a crisis created by Algeria to build a stronger state, which meant that France could end its colonial war and continue its economic growth with stable government. In January 1963 he signed a friendship treaty with Adenauer, a symbol of the reconciliation on which western Europe's recovery rested.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Fourth Republic fell because colonial war exposed its weak executive.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its economic record was strong, so its failure was political, not economic.

argumentsThatWork.claim: De Gaulle used the 1958 crisis to build a strong presidential state.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His return came through army pressure, which raises questions about its legitimacy.

argumentsThatWork.claim: De Gaulle ended the Algerian war against the wishes of those who had brought him to power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Independence was increasingly accepted internationally and by French opinion, so he followed as well as led.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the collapse of the Fourth Republic in 1958.
Examine the role of de Gaulle in ending the Algerian war between 1958 and 1962.

useItInAnEssay.claim: De Gaulle ended the Algerian war by using the authority of the new presidency against those who had brought him to power.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Settlers and soldiers had demanded his return in May 1958, yet in September 1959 he proposed self-determination and faced down the April 1961 putsch.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that only a leader with his prestige and a strong executive could override the army and the settlers, so the Fifth Republic made independence possible.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, French opinion had turned decisively against the war after the putsch, so de Gaulle followed as well as led the country.
useItInAnEssay.judge: De Gaulle's role was therefore decisive in the timing and manner of the settlement, though not in the direction of opinion.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the Marshall Plan responsible for the economic recovery of western Europe between 1947 and 1952?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far the Plan, compared with national policies and world trade, caused recovery

modelPlan.thesis: The Marshall Plan was largely responsible for the speed and political safety of recovery, because it paid for essential imports and bought time; but national planning and world trade drove long-term growth.

arguments.claim: Marshall dollars paid for imports and investment (named factor first).
It bought time for fragile democracies.
National policies: Monnet planning, German currency reform.
European cooperation and world trade.

modelPlan.counter: Judt accepts Europe could have grown without the aid, at the cost of lower living standards.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would recovery have been politically survivable without it? Probably not in 1947, so the Plan was decisive for timing and stability.

segments.text: The Marshall Plan was largely responsible for the speed and political safety of western Europe's recovery.
By 1952 the US had spent about $13 billion, and western Europe's combined GNP rose 30 per cent between 1947 and 1951.
This meant that governments could import food and raw materials without cutting living standards, so they avoided the political crises austerity might have caused.
However, Judt accepts that Europe could probably have grown without the aid, and national plans such as Monnet's shaped how it was used.
The Plan was therefore decisive for how safely Europe recovered, more than for whether it recovered at all.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Adenauer's leadership was the main reason for West Germany's success between 1949 and 1963.” Discuss.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far Adenauer, rather than economics and institutions, explains success

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is partly right: Adenauer anchored West Germany in the West and gave stable leadership, but the economic miracle rested on surviving industry, expellee labour, world trade and institutions designed by others.

arguments.claim: Adenauer's Western anchoring and stable leadership (named factor first).
Institutions designed to avoid Weimar.
The social market and economic foundations.
World trade and exports.

modelPlan.counter: His own party removed him in 1963, suggesting his authority depended on circumstances.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which factor could West Germany least have done without? Economic growth, which gave the new democracy legitimacy; Adenauer made the most of it.

segments.text: Adenauer's leadership was important, but West Germany's success rested more on its economic foundations.
In the 1950s output per head grew 6.5 per cent a year, and West Germany's share of world manufactured exports rose from 7.3 to 19.3 per cent.
This meant that prosperity gave the new democracy legitimacy, so Adenauer governed a country whose citizens associated democracy with success.
However, Judt credits Adenauer with steering between neo-Nazism and neutralism and anchoring West Germany in the West, which made that growth secure.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: Adenauer secured the framework, but the economy delivered the success.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the collapse of the Fourth Republic in 1958.

decodeKey.scope: The collapse of the Fourth Republic
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The Fourth Republic collapsed mainly because the Algerian war exposed its weak executive; its main consequence was a strong presidential republic that could end the war.

arguments.claim: Reason: a weak executive and unstable coalitions.
Reason: the cost and politics of the Algerian war.
Consequence: the Fifth Republic and a strong presidency.
Consequence: the end of the Algerian war.

modelPlan.counter: Judt says the wonder is that the Fourth Republic lasted as long as it did, which suggests its collapse was structural rather than caused by Algeria alone.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence mattered most? The strong presidency, which made the end of the war possible.

segments.text: The Fourth Republic collapsed mainly because the Algerian war exposed its lack of an effective executive.
France lost two-thirds of its currency reserves in 1955–57, and in May 1958 settlers and soldiers in Algiers demanded de Gaulle's return while rebels seized Corsica.
This meant that short-lived coalition governments could neither control the army nor end the war, so the crisis could only be resolved by changing the regime.
However, the Republic's economy was growing, so its failure was political rather than economic.
The main consequence was therefore a strong presidential state, which in turn allowed de Gaulle to end the war.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the recovery of West Germany and France between 1945 and 1963.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The recovery of the two states

modelPlan.thesis: Both recovered fast with Marshall aid and European cooperation, but they differed in method and stability: West Germany grew faster under stable government and a social market, while France planned its modernisation but was destabilised by colonial war until 1958.

arguments.claim: Similarity: Marshall aid and European cooperation.
Similarity: historically high growth in the 1950s.
Difference: social market versus state planning.
Difference: stable Bonn versus the unstable Fourth Republic.

modelPlan.counter: By 1963 France also had stable government, so the political gap closed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Political stability, which shaped how growth was used.

segments.text: West Germany and France both recovered quickly, but under very different political conditions.
West German output per head grew 6.5 per cent a year in the 1950s, against 3.5 per cent in France, whereas the Fourth Republic lost two-thirds of its reserves in 1955–57 to colonial war.
This meant that West Germany's stable institutions let growth translate into legitimacy, while France's growth was undermined by the cost of empire.
However, both relied on Marshall aid and European cooperation, and by 1963 de Gaulle's Fifth Republic had given France stable government too.
The decisive difference before 1958 was therefore political stability, not economic capacity.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the role of de Gaulle in ending the Algerian war between 1958 and 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.scope: The end of the Algerian war
decodeKey.judgement: How far de Gaulle, compared with opinion and international pressure, ended the war

modelPlan.thesis: De Gaulle's role was decisive: he used the authority of the new presidency to override the army and settlers who had brought him to power; but international pressure and French weariness made independence inevitable.

arguments.claim: The strong presidency of the Fifth Republic.
Self-determination proposed in 1959 against settler wishes.
Facing down the barricades, the putsch and the OAS.
International opinion and French weariness.

modelPlan.counter: Opinion in France had turned against the war after the 1961 putsch, so de Gaulle followed as well as led.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could anyone else have ended the war in 1962? Probably not without civil conflict, so his role was decisive in its manner.

segments.text: De Gaulle played the decisive role in ending the Algerian war, because only he could override those who had brought him to power.
Brought back by settlers and soldiers in 1958, he proposed self-determination in September 1959 and faced down the putsch of April 1961.
This meant that the army and settlers lost their claim to speak for France, so negotiations at Evian could produce a ceasefire on 19 March 1962.
However, international opinion favoured independence and most French people concluded after the putsch that Algeria should go, so de Gaulle also followed opinion.
His role was therefore decisive for how and when the war ended, though not for whether Algeria would become independent.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for the West German economic miracle between 1948 and 1963.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason was decisive and how they combined

modelPlan.thesis: The miracle rested mainly on exports in a booming world economy, made possible by surviving industry, expellee labour and the currency reform, and kept stable by the social market and Bonn's institutions.

arguments.claim: Surviving industry and expellee labour.
Exports in a booming world economy.
Marshall aid and European cooperation.
The social market and stable institutions.

modelPlan.counter: The regulated, cartel-like economy suggests policy shaped growth more than free markets did.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason was decisive? Exports, since they turned capacity and labour into growth.

segments.text: The West German economic miracle rested above all on exports in a booming world economy.
West Germany's share of world manufactured exports rose from 7.3 per cent in 1950 to 19.3 per cent in 1960, while output per head grew 6.5 per cent a year.
This meant that surviving factories, such as Volkswagen's, and millions of expellee workers could be put to work selling abroad, so growth fed on itself.
However, the social market and Co-Determination kept industrial peace, which Judt argues let the economic cake grow without conflict.
Exports were therefore the decisive reason, with stable institutions as the condition that let them work.
